name: Magnesium sulfate
high_alert_note: ISMP's 2024 acute-care list explicitly identifies injectable magnesium sulfate as a high-alert medication. This is a medication-safety classification, not a product-specific dosage or administration protocol; local policy controls safeguards. Source classification independently checked; ISMP copyrighted material is cited in the separate evidence audit, not incorporated as a source of medication instructions.
summary: Parenteral magnesium for indicated magnesium deficiency and other formulation-specific indications. Nursing focus: monitor for respiratory and neuromuscular depression, low blood pressure, impaired renal clearance, interaction-related weakness, cardiac-conduction concerns and formulation errors.
evidence_type_note: The evidence here is a regulator product label (prescribing information written for prescribers and pharmacists). It is not a bedside nursing practice guideline: the nursing actions are inferences from label warnings, marked partial, and the unit's protocol governs practice. Targeted 2026-11-21 re-read of the already-registered US Hospira DailyMed label focused on contraindications, drug interactions, adverse effects and symptoms of overdose. This is not a replacement for site-specific bedside procedures.
jurisdiction_note: US FDA label only. EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels were not read; indications, warnings and presentations differ by country and by manufacturer.

items.text: The label indicates magnesium sulfate injection as suitable for replacement therapy in magnesium deficiency, especially in acute hypomagnesaemia accompanied by signs of tetany.
The same Hospira product label also discusses obstetric convulsion indications, but this medication learning record does not provide obstetric treatment pathways or drug dosing.
Watch for the signs of magnesium intoxication, and give particular attention when renal function is impaired.

Check the dispensed magnesium formulation, prescribed route and pharmacy preparation instructions before starting administration. Concentrated products and premixed bags are not interchangeable as ready-to-use preparations; the specific Hospira concentrated syringe label requires preparation before intravenous administration. Never improvise product preparation or administration from this draft.

Review concurrent neuromuscular blockers, sedatives, opioids and anesthetics with the treating team; the magnesium label warns of enhanced neuromuscular blockade and additive CNS/respiratory depression. Follow local monitoring and reporting requirements; do not independently modify doses.
Monitoring of reflexes, respiration, blood pressure and serum magnesium follows the unit's protocol.
The label states that monitoring serum magnesium levels and the clinical state of the patient is essential.

Assess tendon reflexes, respiratory effort and rate, oxygenation, consciousness, blood pressure and heart rhythm as appropriate to the patient's critical illness and prescribed magnesium therapy; a newly absent patellar reflex, respiratory weakness or collapse may herald severe toxicity, especially with reduced renal function.

Check renal function, urine-output trends and ordered serum magnesium concentration; magnesium is primarily cleared by the kidneys and reduced clearance raises the risk of accumulation. The specific frequency and protocol are determined by the clinical team.

Magnesium elimination depends on renal function. Trend urine output and renal results and assess respiratory effort and reflexes. For eclampsia, the registered label calls for injectable calcium rescue treatment to be immediately available; follow the indication-specific toxicity pathway and local emergency preparation policy.
Parenteral use in the presence of renal insufficiency may lead to magnesium intoxication.
Continuous administration beyond several days to pregnant women can lead to hypocalcaemia and bone abnormalities in the fetus.

The specific Hospira US magnesium sulfate injection label lists heart block or myocardial damage as contraindications. Identify conduction disease or cardiac concerns and obtain prescriber/pharmacy confirmation of patient-specific suitability before administration; other indications and formulations may have different labels.

Concurrent neuromuscular-blocking drugs can produce excessive neuromuscular blockade, and sedatives, opioids, barbiturates or anesthetic agents can increase CNS depression. The label also urges special caution with cardiac glycosides because magnesium-toxicity treatment involving calcium may affect cardiac conduction.

The registered source is a concentrated Hospira syringe, not a ready-to-use premixed infusion. Its package labeling requires a pharmacy-controlled preparation step before IV administration; this draft does not give preparation or administration instructions. Confirm product and pharmacy directions to prevent a dangerous formulation mix-up.
Magnesium excess can present with flushing, sweating, hypotension, weakness and diminishing or absent deep-tendon reflexes, progressing to severe neuromuscular depression or flaccid paralysis.

Serious magnesium toxicity may cause CNS depression, marked hypotension/circulatory collapse, cardiac-conduction disturbance and respiratory weakness progressing to respiratory paralysis; unexpected deterioration requires emergency assessment.

The product label reports hypocalcemia with tetany in some obstetric magnesium treatment settings; prolonged maternal exposure may also cause fetal bone abnormalities and neonatal magnesium toxicity. These risks require indication-specific review, not a general ICU electrolyte replacement algorithm.

The specific concentrated product label warns of aluminum accumulation with prolonged parenteral administration in impaired kidney function, particularly in premature neonates. This issue is product-specific and does not establish identical excipient risks for every magnesium preparation.

Immediately report depressed or absent reflexes, decreasing respiratory effort, new oliguria, hypotension, conduction abnormalities or a product error. Activate emergency help for severe respiratory or circulatory compromise and follow the magnesium-toxicity protocol.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record reflexes, respiratory status, blood pressure, laboratory results and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Check reflexes and breathing for signs of magnesium intoxication.
Take extra care when renal function is impaired.
Review serum magnesium and renal function results as ordered.
Report depressed reflexes, weak breathing or hypotension immediately.
Trend urine output and renal function alongside magnesium results, reflexes and breathing; confirm readiness for clinician-directed toxicity treatment under the indication-specific unit protocol.
Recognize a new decrease or loss of deep-tendon reflexes, weakness, altered consciousness or decreasing respiratory effort as potential early signs of magnesium toxicity; report urgently.
Check for new hypotension, conduction abnormalities or clinical deterioration during concurrent magnesium and other drugs affecting neuromuscular function or CNS depression.
Verify whether the supplied product is a concentrated syringe requiring pharmacy-approved preparation or a ready-to-use bag; do not use instructions from one formulation for the other.

Activate local emergency response for severely depressed breathing or circulation in suspected magnesium toxicity; immediately inform the clinician of the drug, product, clinical changes and available serum/renal results.

gaps: Exact dosing, concentration, dilution, infusion rates, drug compatibility and obstetric regimens are deliberately excluded; only validated hospital/pharmacy procedures and the dispensed product's current labeling govern.
Neonatal and obstetric use, and magnesium treatment for rhythm disorders, require specialist protocols not reviewed here.
Different magnesium sulfate formulations, excipients and manufacturers may differ; this record cites one US Hospira product only.
Therapy in severe kidney dysfunction and extracorporeal therapies (CRRT) requires individual renal/pharmacy review; no dose adjustment is taught.
Prescriber-specific toxicity-management decisions (including respiratory support, intravenous calcium rescue and treatment interruption) are not a nursing standing order in this draft.
EMA, MHRA and SFDA labels, local high-alert handling, controlled pharmacy prep and current international magnesium practice guidelines have not been reviewed.
